name: Vendor and tenant COI expiry tracker for small property managers
pain: Property managers track certificates of insurance in hand-updated spreadsheets. Expired COIs go unnoticed until a vendor is on site or a claim lands. Several posters built their own sheet or tool because they couldn't find a decent option.
who_pays: Small and mid property management firms and commercial PMs (roughly 20 to 500 units) that can't get NetVendor or afford enterprise compliance tools.
pay_signal: NetVendor, a paid service, brushed off a new PM who wanted to buy (100). Others run the process by spreadsheet and have for years (110, 112). One manager of 200 units says it is driving them crazy but they lack money for big software (107), which suggests a cheap self-serve tier. Two posters started building their own tool (95, 108).
product_idea: Self-serve web app. Forward or upload COI PDFs and Claude extracts insurer, coverage limits, additional insured and expiry date. The app emails vendors automatically 30 and 7 days before expiry, sends Telegram or email alerts to the PM, and shows a red/green vendor board with an 'OK to dispatch' check. Flat price around $29–79/month by vendor count.
known_competitors: myCOI, TrustLayer, Jones, BCS, PINS, NetVendor, Certificial. Mostly enterprise or sales-led, which leaves room for a cheap self-serve option.
check_next: Read the column list in 95. Check pricing and minimums for TrustLayer, myCOI and BCS. Post a free COI-expiry spreadsheet template plus waitlist in r/propertymanagement to measure signups.

crowding.reason: Several self-serve AI COI trackers already target small property managers at $0–$79/mo (bcs free to 25 vendors, SubDoc $20/mo for 100 vendors, COI File, COISoftware), at or below the proposed price.

name: Recurring compliance and statutory deadline calendar for landlords and PMs
pain: Fire and life-safety inspections (extinguishers, backflow, hood cleaning, alarms) and state legal clocks (deposit return, entry notice, renewal windows) each run on their own cycle. These rules live on state websites or in leases, not in the PM's daily tools. Missed deadlines lead to fines.
who_pays: Small PM firms and landlords running several properties, especially across more than one state.
pay_signal: PMs track these today in spreadsheets and calendar reminders, or rely on the vendor to call (101, 112). Missed inspections are described as causing fines (101). One poster says the lookup takes two minutes but turning it into an action is the unsolved part (113).
product_idea: Per-property compliance calendar. Pick the state and the asset features (sprinklers, kitchen hood, backflow, etc.) and the app generates every recurring due date plus statutory clocks triggered by events (move-out leads to deposit return deadline). Subscribable iCal feed plus Telegram or email alerts. A state-rules database feeds both the app and SEO pages such as '[state] security deposit return deadline'.
known_competitors: Generic PM suites (AppFolio, Buildium) with partial reminders. Facility tools such as BuildingReports and Inspect Point serve vendors rather than PMs. No obvious landlord-focused state-rule calendar.
check_next: Check search volume for 'security deposit return deadline [state]' type queries. Ask in r/propertymanagement and r/Landlord which deadlines they missed last year. Estimate the effort to build a 50-state rules table with Claude and then verify it by hand.

crowding.reason: Search limit hit after one query; UK has several landlord compliance-calendar tools (one free), but no US multi-state competitors or prices could be checked and no proof of payment was found.

name: Statement aggregator for small landlords with multiple managers or portals
pain: Small landlords copy numbers from property management portals and bank apps into Excel every week. One owner of 9 units counted about 600 hours over 3 years. Others check their bank app every morning to see if rent arrived, and they say PM suites are overkill for under 10 units.
who_pays: Landlords and investors with 1–15 units, especially those whose units sit with different property managers.
pay_signal: The 9-unit owner logs 2–4 hours a week by hand (91). Others built their own tool (89) or ask for shared spreadsheets (92). One poster says software ended up more hassle than it was worth for 1–3 units (97). Another forgets to update spreadsheets and wants automatic late-rent detection (99).
product_idea: Owners forward monthly PM statements, PDFs or CSVs to an inbox. Claude parses rent, fees and repairs per unit into one normalized ledger and dashboard. The app sends Telegram or email alerts when expected rent hasn't appeared, plus a year-end Schedule E style export. Priced at about $10–20/month.
known_competitors: Stessa, Baselane, TurboTenant, Landlord Studio, RentRedi. They focus on bank feeds or self-managed rentals, and none clearly parses third-party PM owner statements.
check_next: Collect 10 real owner-statement PDFs from different PM software (AppFolio, Buildium, Rent Manager) and test how accurately Claude extracts them. Ask the author of 91 whether forwarding statements would replace their weekly sheet.

crowding.reason: Rental bookkeeping at $12-35/mo is crowded and Stessa (free tier) already imports AppFolio owner statements; I couldn't check whether other manager systems or emailed PDFs are covered, or find proof anyone pays specifically to combine statements from several managers.

name: Branded monthly owner report generator for small PMs
pain: PMs managing a handful of properties track rent and expenses in spreadsheets, clean them up by hand, reformat them into PDFs and email them to owners every month. The result still looks janky, and they work across Buildium, Gmail and Drive tabs.
who_pays: Small and boutique PMs, either too small for AppFolio or wanting nicer reports than their suite produces.
pay_signal: This is a recurring monthly manual chore described as more effort than it should be (114). PMs already pay for suites such as Buildium but still juggle tools (115). On the receiving side, owners copy those portal numbers back into Excel (91).
product_idea: Upload the month's spreadsheet or a Buildium export. The tool produces a polished branded PDF and web report per owner, with a Claude-written plain-English summary (occupancy, notable repairs, variance vs last month), and batch-emails it to owners. Priced per owner or per door.
known_competitors: Built-in owner statements in AppFolio, Buildium, DoorLoop and Rentvine. Generic report tools such as Databox and Google Looker Studio.
check_next: Ask 114 and similar posters what their export format is and what a 'non-janky' report needs. Test whether a Buildium CSV export has enough fields to build the report.

crowding.reason: Buildium, DoorLoop and Rentvine already include automated, batch-sent monthly owner reports at prices PMs pay; no proof that anyone pays for a separate prettier or AI-written report on top.

name: Fast move-in and move-out walkthrough report builder
pain: Small landlords spend about 20 minutes on site plus 45 minutes at a desk per unit turning walkthrough photos and notes into a finished report. Inspection photos, notes and follow-ups end up scattered across phones, shared folders and spreadsheets.
who_pays: Landlords, short-term rental hosts and small PMs doing turnover and periodic inspections.
pay_signal: One owner of 3 units says paperwork takes hours and asks how managers with 20–50 doors cope (93). Another describes current workarounds of spreadsheets, shared folders and phone camera rolls (103). These are repeated per-turnover chores.
product_idea: Mobile web app. Walk room by room, take photos and dictate voice notes. Claude turns them into a structured condition report with item ratings and repair tasks, then outputs a timestamped PDF the tenant can e-sign. It can compare move-in and move-out reports for deposit disputes.
known_competitors: RentCheck, zInspector, HappyCo, Inspectify, TurboTenant inspection checklists.
check_next: Compare RentCheck and zInspector pricing for small portfolios. Check whether their reviews complain about desk time after the walkthrough, which is the gap a voice-to-report feature would target.

crowding.reason: A dominant free option (TurboTenant condition reports with tenant signing), several established paid tools ($1/door to $89/mo) with move-in/move-out comparison, and AI report builders (InspectAI, Oryon, Property Inspect) already exist; small landlords are told free tiers are enough.

name: Lease abstraction and key-date extraction for small PMs
pain: PMs abstract leases by hand or outsource it. Renewal windows, notice periods and other clauses stay buried in lease PDFs and never reach the PM's spreadsheet or calendar.
who_pays: Commercial and residential PMs and small brokerages handling dozens to hundreds of leases.
pay_signal: One poster asks whether PMs use paid lease abstraction software or a person, in-house or outsourced, which shows existing spend on software or labor (90). Another names the lease-to-workflow gap directly (113).
product_idea: Upload lease PDFs. Claude extracts a standard abstract (rent schedule, escalations, renewal and option dates, notice requirements, CAM terms) into a spreadsheet and calendar feed. Per-lease pricing (for example $3–5 per lease) undercuts outsourced abstraction, with deadline alerts via email or Telegram.
known_competitors: Prophia, LeaseLens, Docsumo, Kira, MRI/Yardi add-ons, and offshore abstraction services. Mostly sales-led.
check_next: Check replies to 90 for what made people drop software. Benchmark Claude extraction accuracy on 5 sample commercial leases. Price-check outsourced per-lease abstraction rates.

name: Stem and multitrack QC checker for engineers
pain: Assistant engineers drag every stem and multitrack into a DAW just to check sync, missing audio, odd stereo exports, mismatched lengths and sloppy naming before sending or starting a mix. One assistant engineer says they spend way too much time on this basic QC step.
who_pays: Mix and assistant engineers, mastering engineers and small studios that already pay for plugins.
pay_signal: A repeated per-project manual chore is described as overkill and a time sink (22). Engineers are building local browser tools for similar repetitive DAW prep (25), which shows appetite. Pay intent has not been stated outright, so validation is needed.
product_idea: Local-only browser tool (Web Audio, nothing uploaded). Drop a folder of stems and it flags sample rate, bit depth or length mismatches, silent or near-silent files, fake stereo, clipping, missing expected instruments and start-offset drift. It also auto-renames to a convention and exports a PDF QC report to send to the client. Freemium with a one-time pro license.
known_competitors: Manual checks in the DAW. Pro QC tools such as Sound Radix and iZotope RX batch processing, plus delivery-QC tools for broadcast (Vidchecker, Baton) that are too heavy for this use. No obvious lightweight stem checker.
check_next: Read the comments on 22 for the workflows mentioned. Prototype a single-page checker and post it in r/audioengineering to measure usage, then ask what checks they would pay for.

crowding.reason: Stem Checker already ships this exact product (macOS app at $3.99/mo or $29.99 lifetime, plus a free browser checker with PDF reports), has been reviewed by Sound On Sound and Production Expert, and your pain quote comes from its own launch thread.

name: Offline drive and footage archive catalog for videographers
pain: Videographers with 20+ archive SSDs and HDDs can't find which drive holds a project without plugging drives in, and they hand-organize files after each shoot. Audio collectors report that spreadsheets break at scale and existing catalog apps cost money or are poor.
who_pays: Wedding and event videographers, small production companies, and audio and sample collectors.
pay_signal: One poster asks how others manage this at scale and lists spreadsheets as an option (35). A post-shoot file-transfer post asks whether people organize by hand or use an automated system (37). An agency has recurring logging errors across batched episodes (58). A developer found existing catalogers either cost money or suck, and built one (8).
product_idea: Desktop app that indexes each drive when connected, capturing clip metadata, thumbnails, camera and date. It produces a searchable offline catalog of all drives and auto-builds a client/project folder structure on ingest with a naming convention. Optional Claude summaries of clip contents from thumbnails. One-time license around $49.
known_competitors: NeoFinder, DiskCatalogMaker, Kyno, Hedge/OffShoot, PostLab, Silverstack.
check_next: Read the top comments on 35 for tool names and complaints, especially about NeoFinder and Kyno. Check whether thumbnail-based search would be a differentiator.

crowding.reason: NeoFinder and DiskCatalogMaker (~$39 one-time, mature) already catalog drives offline, and Tusk targets videographers with offline file tracking plus ingest at $49-$79, the same price as the proposed product.

name: Playlist curator growth tracker and indie release admin
pain: Playlist curators track follower changes and track adds and removals manually in spreadsheets and can't tell what moved numbers. Indie artists spend about 80% of release time on admin (pitch formatting, spreadsheets, curator follow-ups) across Notion, sheets and reminder texts.
who_pays: Independent artists, small managers or labels, and playlist curators who already pay for SubmitHub, Groover and ads.
pay_signal: Artists pay for promo but report wasting about $400 over 8 months (119). They also complain about paid Groover reviews (120). Curators keep manual spreadsheets (128). One artist logged 80% admin time (123). Others ask what tool to use (124) or are building a cheap hub (127).
product_idea: Spotify-API-based curator dashboard. It snapshots playlist followers daily, logs adds and removals, correlates follower changes with specific tracks, and sends Telegram alerts (sudden drop, a track removed from a curator's list). An artist mode tracks pitch status per curator, sends follow-up reminders, and alerts when a pitched track lands on a playlist.
known_competitors: Chartmetric, Soundcharts, Songstats, Playlist Push, Artist.Tools, SubmitHub.
check_next: Check whether follower counts are still exposed for third-party playlists after the Spotify Web API restrictions. Check Artist.Tools and Songstats pricing. DM the poster of 128 and other curators to test willingness to pay $5–10/month.

crowding.reason: Playlist follower history and add/remove alerts are already sold by Songstats, artist.tools, Chartmetric, Soundcharts and SpotOnTrack at $10-$15/mo, which artists accept; the curator track-linking and artist pitch-tracker angles are unchecked and a thin wedge.

name: Gear inventory and job-prep kit lists for videographers
pain: Solo videographers spend hours prepping gear for each job, starting from zero each time, and build inventory spreadsheets by hand for insurance and purchase planning.
who_pays: Solo and small-crew videographers and photographers carrying insured gear.
pay_signal: One videographer says prep takes hours every job (56). Another is building a gear inventory spreadsheet for insurance, noting the value adds up fast (41). A small production company is investing in carts to speed hauling (45). Explicit software pay intent is not shown, so this is a weaker signal.
product_idea: Mobile-friendly app. Add gear once (Claude autofills specs and value from the model name) and build reusable kit templates per job type ('wedding', 'interview'). Check items out and in per job with QR labels, and export an insurance schedule PDF. Freemium, with pro at $5/month.
known_competitors: Cheqroom, Sortly, Shelf.nu, Kitsplit, Gear Patrol-style spreadsheet templates.
check_next: Read the replies to 56 and 41 for which tools people use. Test demand cheaply with a paid Notion or Sheets gear-and-kit template on Gumroad before building an app.

crowding.reason: GearDex already ships nearly the exact feature set (inventory, kits, packing manifests, QR labels, AI price lookup, insurance records) at $3.25-4/mo with a free tier, plus several free apps (MyGearVault, Camera Shelf, onurgear); no sourced proof that solo videographers pay more.
